data.title: Local Privilege Escalation via Sudo Misconfiguration
data.summary:
The sudo configuration permitted standard users to execute commands as root that
provide a route to an interactive shell, allowing complete control of the
affected hosts.
data.description:
The sudo configuration on the affected systems granted standard user accounts the
ability to run specific commands with root privileges. The intention in such
configurations is to delegate a narrow administrative task without granting full
administrative access.

The commands permitted, however, provide functionality that can be used to obtain
an interactive shell. A wide range of ordinary utilities offer this capability
directly or indirectly, including editors that can spawn subprocesses,
interpreters that execute arbitrary code, pagers that invoke a shell, archive
tools that execute filters, and any utility accepting a user-controlled
configuration file. Where such a command is permitted, the delegation is
equivalent to granting unrestricted root access.

The use of wildcards in the configuration extends this further, as the pattern
frequently matches argument combinations the author did not anticipate, including
paths that permit arbitrary files to be read or written as root.

Where the NOPASSWD directive is also present, escalation requires no knowledge of
the user's own password, so any compromise of the account - including through a
service running under it - immediately becomes full compromise of the host.

Escalation to root was confirmed during testing.
data.impact:
An attacker holding access to any affected user account could obtain complete
control of the host. This permits access to all data held on the system, the
recovery of credentials stored in configuration files and process memory, the
installation of persistence, and the modification of logs to conceal the
activity. Where credentials recovered are valid elsewhere, the compromise extends
beyond the affected host.
data.recommendation:
1. Review the sudo configuration on all systems and remove entries granting
   commands that can be used to obtain a shell or to read and write arbitrary
   files as root.

2. Verify each permitted command against a reference of known escalation
   techniques, such as the GTFOBins project, before including it in the
   configuration.

3. Avoid wildcards in command specifications. Where a task requires arguments
   that vary, implement it as a dedicated script owned by root and not writable
   by the delegated user, and grant sudo access to that script alone.

4. Remove the NOPASSWD directive except where a documented operational
   requirement exists, so that escalation requires the user's own password.

5. Enable sudo command logging and forward the logs to a central system outside
   the host, so that a compromise of the host does not permit the record to be
   altered.

6. Review delegations periodically, as sudo entries added to resolve a specific
   operational problem are rarely removed once the problem has passed.
affected_components: <HOSTNAME> (<IP>) - user <USERNAME> permitted to run <COMMAND> as root
